title: ‘Tulip mania’ probably wasn’t the disaster the legend says
body: The story goes that in 1637 Dutch tulip bulbs sold for the price of houses, then crashed and ruined the economy. Prices for some rare bulbs really did soar and then collapse in February 1637. But historian Anne Goldgar, studying archived contracts, found the trade was limited to a fairly small group of merchants and skilled craftsmen, and the episode did little lasting harm to the booming Dutch economy.

slides.heading: Where the legend came from
slides.text: Much of the lore traces to moralising pamphlets of the time and to Charles Mackay’s 1841 book Extraordinary Popular Delusions and the Madness of Crowds.

slides.prompt: The most prized tulips had flame-like streaks. What caused them?
slides.detail: Found centuries later, the virus ‘broke’ the colour into streaks that made the bulbs striking and hard to propagate, which is why they fetched such prices.

slides.heading: Why bulbs were pricey
slides.text: The most prized ‘broken’ tulips had flame-like streaks caused, as was found centuries later, by a virus, which made them striking and hard to propagate.

slides.heading: Still debated
slides.text: Some economists, like Peter Garber, argue prices were less irrational than they look; others see a true bubble. Either way, the damage was far smaller than the legend.
